newsitem.title: USA: Bias suit vs. R.R. Donnelley may take years - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Bias suit vs. R.R. Donnelley may take years - lawyer.

text.p: The lawyer who filed a $500 million lawsuit charging R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co. with racial discrimination expects a formal answer from the company in a few weeks but said the case may take years to resolve.
"Most of these cases go on for years because of the paperwork and documents involved," Chicago attorney H. Candace Gorman said in a telephone interview.

The class-action lawsuit, filed in federal court in Chicago on Monday, alleges the world's largest commercial printer discriminated against black employees when arranging transfers to other jobs in 1993 related to a plant closing.
The suit lists 22 blacks who were former Donnelley employees as plaintiffs and seeks $500 million in damages.

The suit came less than two weeks after Texaco Inc. agreed to pay $176 million to settle a racial bias suit in the biggest discrimination settlement in the United States. A boycott against Texaco is continuing because the nation's third-largest oil company has made little progress improving its minority policies, minority groups said on Tuesday.
Donnelley said it was "outraged" over the lawsuit and denied any racial bias.

"We can categorically deny any pattern or process of racial discrimination associated with the closing of the plant," the company said. It decided to shut the Chicago plant after Sears, Roebuck & Co. stopped printing its catalogue.
One financial analyst who has followed Chicago-based Donnelley for years said, "My sense is Donnelley was employee-friendly and fairly inclusive in its policies. They really have stressed diversity."
Gorman said the class-action suit, covering about 600 people, had been in the works for some time.

"R.R. Donnelley used race as a criteria for deciding which permanent employees would be transferred to other locations and which would be terminated" after the 1993 announcement that the plant would be closed, the suit said.

The suit said only seven of the plant's 575 black employees, or 1.2 percent, were eventually transferred to other locations. It said 31 percent of white employees affected were transferred. Donnelley closed the plant in December 1994.
"The statistical likelihood of this phenomena occurring by chance is substantially less than one in one trillion," the complaint alleged.
The complaint also said "management at R.R. Donnelley consistently referred to the high number of African-Americans at the Chicago division as the 'black problem'."

It further stated that Donnelley classified as "temporary" many employees who worked for the company for as long as 15 to 20 years. It said 94.3 percent of the "temporary" employees at the Chicago division were blacks in January 1993.
Gorman said a complaint filed against Donnelley for alleged age discrimination and violations of pension laws was pending.
"Race discrimination is going on in corporate America all over the place, some subtle and some not so subtle like Texaco Inc. and Donnelley. It's outrageous."
R.R. Donnelley stock added 12.5 cents to $33.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
